summary: Describes a framework for preparing Unicode text strings so that input and comparison behave sensibly for users worldwide. It is useful for identifiers, names and internationalized domain names, but does not itself say how protocols should prepare strings; individual protocols define profiles. It was replaced by RFC 7564.

eli5.summary: People write the same word in many look-alike ways. Stringprep is a recipe for cleaning up text so computers treat words that look the same as the same. It was later replaced by RFC 7564.

questions: what are the steps of stringprep
why does stringprep use normalization form kc
subtitle: A four-step recipe for cleaning up Unicode text so that strings people type can be compared sensibly.

tldr.problem: Internationalized text can be typed and displayed in many ways, so two people who think they entered the same string can produce different characters.
tldr.mechanism: Stringprep defines a framework that maps characters, optionally normalizes with Unicode form KC, rejects prohibited characters and optionally checks bidirectional text. Each protocol picks its options in a profile.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3454 is a framework, not a complete protocol, and is obsoleted by RFC 7564.

today: RFC 3454 was a Proposed Standard published in December 2002 and is now obsoleted by RFC 7564. Read the newer RFC for current guidance.

sections.title: The Problem and the Goal
sections.content:
Applications can display text in many ways, and users can enter it in a myriad of fashions. That makes it hard to compare internationalized text, meaning text that is not limited to US-ASCII, in a consistent way. Stringprep is a framework of processing rules for Unicode text. The goal is that if two people enter what they think is the same string using two different input mechanisms, the strings match character by character.

A profile can also exclude characters that should not normally appear in a protocol's text. For example, because a backspace character can cause unpredictable display results, a profile can make a string containing one an error. A profile turns one input string into one output string, or returns an error. It never does both.

The framework has limits. It does not describe how data is transcoded from other character sets into Unicode, and it cannot make spelling variants such as "theater" and "theatre" equivalent.
sections.eli5: Imagine two kids write the same name but one uses fancy letters. Stringprep tidies both names so a computer sees them as the same. It cannot fix different spellings, though.

sections.title: The Four Preparation Steps
sections.content:
Preparing a string takes four steps, and they MUST be done in this order:

  1. Map: replace each character that has a mapping with its mapping.
  2. Normalize: optionally apply Unicode normalization.
  3. Prohibit: if any character that is not allowed in the output is found, return an error.
  4. Check bidi: optionally check right-to-left characters and return an error if the string breaks the bidirectional rules.

Mapping and normalization can be one-to-none, one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one or many-to-many, so the output can be shorter or longer than the input. Systems that use stringprep MUST be ready for that. Mapped characters are not scanned again during mapping.
sections.eli5: It is like washing vegetables: swap, tidy, throw out anything bad, then do one last check. The order matters.

sections.title: Mapping, Normalization and Prohibited Output
sections.content:
The mapping tables are in appendix B. Table B.1 lists characters that are simply deleted because their presence or absence should not make two identifiers different, such as 00AD SOFT HYPHEN, 200B ZERO WIDTH SPACE and the variation selectors. For case-insensitive comparison, a profile SHOULD use Table B.2 (when it also uses Unicode normalization form KC) or Table B.3 (when it uses no normalization). Both map uppercase to lowercase, because Internet protocols traditionally use lowercase.

A profile may use no normalization or Unicode normalization form KC. If a profile normalizes, it MUST use form KC, which maps many compatibility characters to their equivalents. Without normalization, the results can surprise users, depending on how they enter text.

Before output, text MUST be checked for prohibited code points. The appendix C tables cover space characters, control characters, private use, non-character code points, surrogate codes, characters inappropriate for plain text or canonical representation, characters that change display properties or are deprecated, and tagging characters. A profile may use all or some of these tables and may prohibit more.
sections.eli5: First the recipe throws away invisible bits and makes every letter small. Then it makes look-alike characters the same kind. Finally it rejects anything on a banned list, like spaces or weird control symbols.

sections.title: Profiles, Bidirectional Text and Unassigned Code Points
sections.content:
Stringprep does not stand alone. A protocol must define a profile that states the intended applicability, the character repertoire (Unicode 3.2 for this version), the mapping tables, the normalization used, the prohibited tables, the bidirectional testing and any additional prohibited characters. Each profile MUST be registered with IANA after IESG review, and developers are strongly encouraged to reuse existing profiles.

Bidirectional checking is optional but strongly considered. A profile that uses it MUST prohibit the section 5.8 characters, MUST NOT allow a string with any right-to-left character (RandALCat) to also contain a left-to-right (LCat) character, and MUST make the first and last characters right-to-left when any are present.

Code points not assigned in the profile's repertoire are called unassigned. Stored strings MUST NOT contain them, but queries MAY. This avoids needing a versioning protocol as Unicode grows. Stored strings in structures that cannot change, such as the signed parts of digital certificates, MUST NOT contain any unassigned code points.
sections.eli5: The recipe is a basic cookbook, and each protocol writes its own menu from it. Reading right-to-left words has extra rules so that text cannot trick the eye.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Stringprep does nothing to map similar-looking characters together or to prohibit characters because they look like others. User applications can help by showing when a string changes between scripts. Protocols that forbid certain characters or sequences MUST check for them after stringprep processing, because stringprep can change the input.

If the bidirectional requirements are not used, many strings with characters in a different order can display identically, which can confuse users. Invisible code points that are not mapped out or prohibited can make two identical-looking strings fail to match.

The RFC also warns that all programs should reject illegal or ill-formed UTF-8 or UTF-16 sequences. Normalization and encoding conversion can make strings grow or shrink, so fixed-size buffers can fail insecurely.
sections.eli5: Some letters look alike, and stringprep does not catch those tricks. Programs must also be careful that cleaned-up text can come out longer or shorter than it went in.
